title: Interpreting and Communicating Technical Information

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Skateboarders say "ollie" and "grind." To another skater those words are fast and exact; to someone outside the group they are noise. Jargon is the same trade shorthand for a profession. The skill is not avoiding it — it is checking whether the listener has the same shorthand loaded, and unpacking the term when they do not.

### Question 2

When a friend asks how to get to your place, you answer differently depending on whether they are walking, driving, or new to the city. The address never changes; the route description does. Audience analysis is finding out who the traveler is before you draw the map, so you spend your words on what they actually lack.

### Question 3

Plain language is handing someone a clear glass of water instead of a muddy one. Same water, but now they can see through it. Nothing is removed from the content — the sentence still says exactly what to do — you have only taken out the sediment that made the reader stop and re-read.

### Question 4

The original takes a straight road and adds detours. The fix has two moves you can reuse anywhere: turn thing-words back into action-words ("ingestion" becomes "eating"), and name the person doing the action ("you"). Also notice why the negative version still fails — telling someone what not to do leaves them to guess what to do.

### Question 5

Take a film. A summary is telling a friend the whole plot in three sentences. A paraphrase is retelling one scene in your own words, beat by beat, so nothing in that scene is lost. Both are still someone else's story, which is why the citation stays attached either way — changing the words does not change whose ideas they are.

### Question 6

If a recipe said "add the sugar," then "add the sweetener," then "add the white stuff," you would start counting how many bags to buy. In narrative writing, varying your words is style. In instructions, varying your words looks like a new ingredient appeared. Name it once, pair it with the familiar term, then keep saying the same name.

### Question 7

"Dog" and "mutt" point at the same animal — that shared pointing is denotation. "Mutt" also drags a judgment along with it, and that extra freight is connotation. Every content word is a package: the label tells you what is inside, the wrapping tells you how to feel about it, and in charting you often want the plainest wrapping available.

### Question 8

Describing a graph is saying "the line goes down." Interpreting it is saying "fewer people got infections, and the drop lines up with the new handwashing program." Two traps sit on either side: saying too little (just reading the axes back) and saying too much (promising the line keeps falling forever). Interpretation lands between them.

### Question 9

If your kitchen were on fire you would not open the 911 call with "we bought this house in 2019." You would say where the fire is. Urgent messages run most-important-first, backstory second, because the listener can always ask for more history but cannot recover a point they never heard.

### Question 10

Ask someone "got it?" and they will say yes, because saying no feels like admitting failure. Ask them to walk you back through the route and you find out in ten seconds exactly where it went sideways. Teach-back moves the test from politeness to performance, and a wrong answer is feedback on your explanation, not on the patient.

### Question 11

"Students who eat breakfast tend to earn higher grades" is not "breakfast makes you smart." The first says two things travel together; the second says one drives the other, and it promises it works for you. Hedges like "tend to" and "associated with" are the honesty dial on a claim, so deleting them is not tightening the prose — it is changing what was claimed.

### Question 12

Good museums post a family guide and a specialist guide beside the same exhibit, each clearly signed, so nobody wades through the wrong one. Mixing them into one paragraph is a tour guide alternating between baby talk and a lecture mid-sentence. The document does not have to pick a reader — it has to label its doors so each reader can pick a section.
